# How to Create AI-Generated Podcasts in 2026

You do not need a studio, an engineer, or even flawless audio to start a podcast in 2026. What you need is a repeatable workflow. The tools below each own one step, and together they turn a laptop and a microphone into a publishable show. Follow the order — skipping a step early just creates rework later.

## Step 1: Plan the episode

Before recording, structure the conversation. Upload your research, guest bio, and outline to [[link:/tools/1500|NotebookLM]] (Google's source-grounded assistant) to generate a tight run-of-show with citations you can trust. It keeps you from ad-libbing into dead air and gives you factual anchors to return to.

## Step 2: Record with clean separate tracks

If you have remote guests, record locally. [[link:/tools/1549|Riverside]] captures separate local audio and video tracks per guest, so a bad connection on their end does not ruin your master. It also transcribes the session, which you will want in step four.

## Step 3: Clean the audio

Even good mics pick up room noise. [[link:/tools/1535|Adobe Podcast AI]] removes background noise and lifts voice quality to near-studio levels from any microphone. Run every raw track through it before editing — it is the difference between "homemade" and "professional" to a listener's ear.

## Step 4: Edit by editing the transcript

[[link:/tools/79|Descript]] lets you cut audio by deleting words in a transcript: remove filler words, tighten tangents, and even overdub with a cloned voice for a pickup line instead of re-recording. This step is where episodes actually get good, and it is far faster than waveform editing.

## Step 5: Add a host voice or narration

Need an intro, ad read, or narration you did not record? [[link:/tools/78|Murf AI]] generates a consistent professional voice in 20+ languages with controllable tone — handy for recurring segments. Use it sparingly so the show still sounds human.

## Step 6: Publish and repurpose

Export, upload to your host, and clip highlights for social. The transcript from step two feeds those clips.

Best for aspiring podcasters and teams shipping a show without a production budget. Avoid over-automating the host voice — listeners stay for people, not for synthetic narration.

## Your first episode, end to end

A realistic timeline removes the intimidation. Day one: outline in [[link:/tools/1500|NotebookLM]] from your research. Day two: record remotely in [[link:/tools/1549|Riverside]], even if it is just you and one guest. Day three: clean every track with [[link:/tools/1535|Adobe Podcast AI]] and edit by transcript in [[link:/tools/79|Descript]], cutting filler and tightening. Day four: add an intro or segment with [[link:/tools/78|Murf AI]] if needed, export, and write the show notes from the transcript. Day five: publish and clip highlights for social.

The mistake is skipping the clean step. Homemade audio is forgiven; muddy audio is not. A single pass through a noise remover is the cheapest quality upgrade in podcasting, and it is the difference between a show people finish and one they bounce from.

## The monetization reality

Do not expect revenue from episode one. Podcasts compound: the AI workflow gets you publishing consistently, and consistency is what builds an audience you can later monetize. The biggest lever [[link:/tools/79|Descript]] and [[link:/tools/1549|Riverside]] give you is repurposing — clip every episode into social posts so each one markets the next. Treat the show as a long-game asset, not a quick income stream.

## Structuring an episode people finish

Retention, not downloads, is the signal worth chasing. Open with a ten-second cold open — the most surprising moment from the episode, not "welcome to the show" — then state what the listener will get and by when. Break the middle into two or three named segments so the transcript in [[link:/tools/79|Descript]] gives you obvious cut points, and close by restating the single takeaway. Length matters less than density: a tight eighteen minutes beats a wandering fifty. When you edit, cut the tangents that served the conversation but not the listener, and keep one or two imperfect moments. Over-polished shows sound synthetic, which is precisely the criticism AI-assisted production invites.

One more step pays for itself: turn each episode into written material. The transcript is already structured, and [[link:/tools/1105|Castmagic]] generates show notes, timestamps, and social clips from it, which removes the hour of writing that makes most new shows stop after episode four. Skim for accuracy before publishing — the summary is only as good as the transcript.

## FAQ

**Do I need all five tools?** No. A minimal setup is Riverside (or any recorder) plus Descript plus Adobe Podcast AI. NotebookLM and Murf are upgrades, not requirements.

**Is AI narration acceptable to listeners?** For intros, ads, and translations, yes. For the core host conversation, human voice builds more trust.

**Can I record solo without guests?** Absolutely. Steps 3-5 (clean, edit by transcript, add segments) apply to solo shows too.

**What about music and rights?** Use licensed or royalty-free beds; AI voice tools generate speech, not cleared music, so source music separately.

**How long should an episode be?** As long as it stays interesting. Eighteen tight minutes beats a wandering hour; the transcript shows you where a listener would have left, which is the most honest editor you have.

**Can AI write my show notes?** Yes. The transcript is already structured material — tools like Castmagic turn it into notes, timestamps, and clips. Edit for accuracy before you publish.
